newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: State measures may not cure S.Korea economic woes.
newsitem.headline: State measures may not cure S.Korea economic woes.

text.p: Measures to boost South Korea's industrial competitiveness are unlikely to cure the country's economic ills, economic analysts warned on Sunday.

"The government has a good reason to be alarmed about the current economic slowdown. But government intervention only disrupts price mechanisms," said Kim Joon-il, a researcher at the Korea Development Institute (KDI).

Government planners have drawn up a blueprint to make industrial inputs cheaper and reduce the cost of funds after corporate profits were slashed by plunging prices for semiconductors, petrochemicals and steel products -- South Korea's major exports.
As a result, the nation's trade deficit is snowballing and could exceed $20 billion this year, compared with $10 billion in 1995.
Earlier this month the finance ministry said it would cut domestic steel prices, freeze wage levels for senior government officials and open power production to private-sector competition.
It also said the government would make it easier for big companies to borrow money from overseas.
On Thursday, the central Bank of Korea announced cuts in bank reserve requirements to an average of 5.5 percent from 7.4 percent, a step that will lead to interest rate cuts.
On Wednesday the ministry of information and communications said that long-distance, international and cellular call service charges would be lowered by 10 to 15 percent, effective December 1.

But Yoo Won-bae, an economic professor at Sukmyung University was sceptical about the measures' effectiveness. "The government cannot boost private-sector competitiveness simply by strengthening its support," he said.
South Korea has said the wider trade deficit would limit economic growth this year to about seven percent, down from nine percent last year.

The government has said the economic downturn stems from structural weakness -- low efficiency and high costs -- and boosting efficiency through cost-cutting and privatisation has become a matter of urgency.
"The government will economise on the state budget and promote the privatisation programme as scheduled," President Kim Young-sam said in a speech delivered to the National Assembly.
President Kim said the government would cut staffing in the state sector. It will also try to bring down high wages, interest rates and distribution costs to improve productivity.
Government support would be expanded to help small companies' restructuring efforts, he added.

In compliance with the government's belt-tightening drive, the Korea Employers' Federation said earlier this month it would recommend to its money-losing members that they freeze wages for grassroots workers and executives next year. More than 4,000 companies are registered as members of the federation.
"Wage increases should be supported by improving productivity," said a federation official.
But analysts said the decision could face resistance from the nation's often militant labour groups.
"Talk of wage freezes could play against productivity," said Professor Yoon.
